Part 1: understand what [top model] is for

01. What it sees, and what it cannot

Let me kill the biggest misunderstanding first.

[top model] has no search volume. It has no live top 10. It has no backlink graph. It does not see your Search Console, your Analytics or your server logs. Out of the box, it knows how SEO works. It does not know how YOUR site is doing.

Ask it "what keywords should I target for my bakery website" with nothing attached, and you get a confident, well-written list of nothing. It will sound like a senior SEO. It will have the data of a horoscope.

So the rule of this whole guide is simple:

  • [top model] never guesses data.
  • You hand it files: a Search Console export, a saved results page, a crawl, a list of your pages.
  • [top model] does the thinking on top: what matters, what to fix first, what to leave alone.

That split is the whole game. The data is cheap and you already have most of it. The thinking is what you used to pay a consultant for.

Where do the files come from?

  • Search Console: Performance, last 28 days, tab Queries and tab Pages, Export. Free. Or the API if you are comfortable with it, because the export only gives you queries OR pages, while the API gives you query AND page on the same row. That second version is what makes step 11 work.
  • The live top 10: search the keyword in a private window, set to the country you target, and save the page. Or use any SERP API.
  • A crawl: Screaming Frog (free up to 500 URLs), or even your sitemap and a script.
  • Your pages: the HTML, or just copy the text of each page into a file.

Put them in one folder. Open Claude Code in that folder. That is the setup.

What a good data folder looks like, for a normal site:

  • /data/gsc/queries-pages.tsv: one row per query and page, with clicks, impressions, CTR and position. A few hundred to a few thousand rows.
  • /data/gsc/pages-previous.csv: the same 28 days one period earlier, for step 14.
  • /data/serp/<keyword>.md: one file per important keyword, the top 10 titles and URLs, in order.
  • /data/crawl/urls.txt and the HTML of your important pages.
  • /data/business.md: 10 lines on what you sell, to whom, and which pages make money.

That last file is the one people forget, and it changes everything. Without it, [top model] optimises for traffic. With it, [top model] optimises for traffic that buys. A query with 40,000 impressions from people who will never pay you is worth less than a query with 400 impressions from people with a credit card in hand.

You do not need all of it for step 11. The first file is enough to start.

Spoiler: its verdict was not the one I expected, and it was more honest than I would have been.

03. "Isn't it just an expensive [advanced model]?"

It is expensive per token. $8 per million tokens in, $40 per million out. Fast mode doubles it.

That is why 49% of people never touch it. They look at the price per token and go back to whatever they used before.

But the price per token is the wrong number. The right one is the price per finished job.

Anthropic's own early testing put [top model] at high effort roughly level with [advanced model] at its maximum effort, for about half the cost. That test was on code, not SEO, so take it as a direction, not a promise. But the logic transfers.

An SEO audit is exactly the kind of job where a weaker model makes you pay twice:

  • It reads 400 rows of Search Console and quietly skips half of them.
  • It trusts the average position Google gives you, which is often wrong (you will see a real case in step 11).
  • It recommends "add more content" to a page whose real problem is the title.
  • And then you spend an hour checking its work, which was the job you wanted to hand off.

A model that gets the diagnosis right the first time is cheaper than a model that is cheap per token. That is the whole price argument.

And for the jobs where it does NOT get you a better answer, you do not use it at all. That is step 04.

04. Which Claude does which SEO job

This is how I split the work. It is my setup, not a benchmark, so adjust it to your own results:

  • [top model]: the thinking. Prioritising 400 queries, diagnosing a traffic drop, reviewing a content plan, deciding what NOT to do. Anything where one wrong assumption wastes a week.
  • [advanced model]: the checking. Reviewing a rewritten page against its brief, catching the claim the writer made up, re-reading a plan before it ships.
  • [mid model]: the hands. Crawling, pulling data, extracting titles and headings from 50 pages, writing first drafts, rewriting meta descriptions at scale.
  • [light model]: the bulk. Sorting 5,000 keywords by intent, tagging pages by type, cleaning an export, deduplicating a list.

The second mistake from the intro is right here. People run [top model] on keyword lists. Tagging 5,000 keywords by intent is not a thinking job. It is a sorting job, and [light model] does it well for a fraction of the price.

Using [top model] to tag 5,000 keywords is like paying a senior consultant to do data entry.

Using [light model] to decide your SEO strategy is worse. You get a strategy that looks fine and is built on nothing.

A quick test to know which model a job needs: if you could hand the job to an intern with a clear checklist, it is [light model] or [mid model]. If you would only trust it to your best senior, it is [top model].

Part 2: set it up at 100%

05. Effort: the setting nobody touches

[top model] has effort levels. Medium is the default in the Claude apps and in Claude Code. Most people never change it.

For SEO work (long jobs, many files, many steps), Anthropic's own guide recommends high.

In Claude Code:

claude --model [top model] --effort high

How I use the levels:

  • Medium: a quick question. "Is this title better than that one?" "What does this error in Search Console mean?"
  • High: anything that touches more than one page or more than one file. Audits, keyword maps, content refreshes, the prompts of Part 4.
  • Higher than high: I almost never need it for SEO. The extra thinking goes into edge cases that do not change the decision.

Effort is also how you control cost. Medium on a small question costs a few cents. High on a 400-row analysis is where the model earns its price.

06. One SEO CLAUDE.md

Claude Code reads a file called CLAUDE.md at the start of every session, from the folder you open it in. Whatever you put there, [top model] follows, every time, without you repeating it.

This is the file that turns a general model into YOUR senior SEO. Here is mine, cleaned up so you can copy it. This is prompt 1:

# SEO rules for this project

Site: example.com. Market: US. Language: English.
Business: [one line: what you sell, to whom].
Money pages: [the 5 URLs that make you money].
Competitors: [3 domains you lose to on Google].

Data
- Never invent a search volume, a position, a click or a backlink. If a number is not in a file here, write "unknown".
- Search Console exports are in /data/gsc, saved SERPs in /data/serp, the crawl in /data/crawl.
- Never trust average position alone: check it against the live SERP file when there is one.
- Always say which file a number comes from.

How to work
- Sort opportunities by impressions first, then by business value. Ignore branded queries.
- One page per search intent. Two pages on the same intent = say it, with both URLs.
- A recommendation names the page, the number behind it and the exact change.
- Prefer fixing an existing page to creating a new one.
- Say when a problem is not worth fixing.

Output
- Blunt. No intro, no politeness, no "great question".
- Tables when there are more than 5 items.
- End with the 3 actions to do first, in order, and what each one should change.

Why each block matters:

  • The business block stops the most common AI SEO mistake: recommending keywords nobody who buys from you would type.
  • The data block is the anti-hallucination block. "Write unknown" is the most useful sentence in the file. Without it, a model fills the gap with a plausible number.
  • "Never trust average position alone" is there because of what you will see in step 11.
  • "Say when a problem is not worth fixing" is the senior SEO sentence. Juniors fix everything. Seniors fix the 3 things that move the curve.

You write it once. Every prompt below gets shorter because of it.

07. What to delete from your old prompts

[top model] follows instructions very literally. That is great when your instructions are clear. It is a problem when your prompts are full of tricks from 2024.

Delete these:

  • "You are the world's best SEO expert with 20 years of experience." The CLAUDE.md already does that job, with real context instead of a costume.
  • "THINK STEP BY STEP", in capitals. High effort already makes it think. And capital letters make it over-apply your rule everywhere, including where it does not fit.
  • "Be thorough. Don't miss anything." It does not know what "thorough" means for you. Say what done looks like instead: "every page in the file has a verdict", "stop when the 20 pages are checked".
  • "Give me 50 keyword ideas." A number of ideas is not a goal. Ask for the decisions instead: "the 5 keywords worth a new page, and why".
  • Long lists of "don'ts". Say what you want it to do. A model told 15 things not to do spends its attention on the 15 things.

Keep these:

  • The files. Always the files.
  • One clear job per prompt.
  • The format of the output you want.
  • The stop condition.

That is it. The prompts in Part 4 are short on purpose.

Part 3: [top model] as the brain, not the hands

08. Brain, not hands

This is the part most people skip, and it is where [top model] pays for itself.

Anthropic writes it plainly in its prompting guide: early testers had good results with [top model] as the planner and orchestrator for other models. And in the same guide: subagents can account for a large part of what a session costs, so check which model your subagents use by default.

Translated for SEO:

  • [top model] decides what to look at.
  • Cheaper models do the fetching, the extracting and the typing.
  • [top model] reads what comes back and judges it.

Think of a real SEO agency. The senior consultant does not open 50 pages one by one to copy their titles into a spreadsheet. A junior does that. The senior reads the spreadsheet and says "these three pages are the problem, here is why".

Same thing here. You pay [top model] prices only for the part that needs [top model].

And watch the second sentence of that guide. If you start subagents without saying which model they run on, they may run on the expensive one. Always name the model in the prompt.

09. [mid model] crawls and writes, [top model] reviews

The simplest version of the team has two models. This is prompt 2:

You are the lead SEO on this audit. Do not crawl or write yourself.

1. Plan: from /data/crawl/urls.txt, pick the pages worth checking (max 30) and say why for each.
2. For each page, start a subagent on [mid model] that returns: URL, title, H1, word count, main search intent, internal links in and out.
3. Read every return. Reject and rerun any return that guesses a number.
4. Your output: the 10 problems that cost the most clicks, page by page, with the fix.
Stop when all 30 pages have a return you accepted.

What this gives you:

  • [top model] spends its tokens on the plan (step 1) and the judgment (steps 3 and 4).
  • [mid model] does the reading, which is most of the volume.
  • Step 3 is the one people forget. A model that reviews the work of another model catches the made-up word counts and the "intent: unclear" lazy answers. That review is the senior's job.

Run it on a small site first. 30 pages is enough to see if the output is useful before you spend more.

10. A 4-model audit team

When the site is bigger, give each model its own lane. This is prompt 3:

Run this SEO audit as a team. You ([top model]) plan and decide. Nobody else decides.

- [light model] subagents: tag every query in /data/gsc/queries.csv by intent (info, compare, buy, brand).
- [mid model] subagents: for the 20 pages with the most impressions, extract title, H1, main intent and their top 3 queries.
- [advanced model] subagent: check each [mid model] extraction against the page HTML in /data/crawl. Flag every mismatch.
- You: compare the intent of the queries with the intent of the pages. List every page where they do not match, with the numbers.

Stop when each of the 20 pages has a verdict: keep, fix the title, fix the content, merge, or new page.

Why this order:

  • [light model] tags first, because tagging thousands of queries is volume, not judgment.
  • [mid model] extracts, because reading 20 pages is reading, not judgment.
  • [advanced model] checks [mid model], because extraction errors are where audits quietly go wrong.
  • [top model] decides, because "this page answers the wrong question" is the only call in the list that needs a senior.

The verdict list at the end is the important bit. "Keep, fix the title, fix the content, merge, new page" forces a decision on every page. An audit without a decision is a report you will not read.

Part 4: the prompts

Prompts 1 to 3 are in steps 06, 09 and 10. Here are the other 7, starting with the one I ran this morning.

11. The Search Console quick-win prompt

A quick win is a query where Google already shows you a lot and almost nobody clicks. You are on the page. You are just not chosen.

First, the data. Export your queries AND pages from Search Console, last 28 days. If you can, get them on the same row (the API does it). [top model] needs to know which page shows up for what.

This is our table, sorted by impressions:

Look at the top: 48,819 people saw us on "semrush alternatives". 1 clicked. And "semrush alternative", singular, same page: 5,454 impressions and 16 clicks. Keep that detail in mind.

Then I read the live Google top 10 for the 3 biggest queries and saved it in a file. Here is "semrush alternatives" this morning:

And "ahrefs alternatives":

Then prompt 4, with both files in the folder:

You are a senior SEO. Files here: queries-pages.tsv (Google Search Console, last 28 days: query, page, clicks, impressions, ctr, position) and serp.md (the live Google top 10 for my 3 biggest queries).

Find my SEO quick wins: queries with many impressions and few clicks.
Rules: sort by impressions, ignore branded queries, never trust average position alone.
For each of the top 5: the page, the numbers, what the live top 10 shows that my result does not, and a new title tag under 60 characters.
Then, in ONE sentence, the single biggest reason I get seen and not clicked.
Be blunt. Only facts from the files. Under 350 words.

Here is its answer, unedited except its closing summary line, which I quote right after. High effort, 1 minute 55 seconds:

1. semrush alternatives, /blog/free-semrush-alternative: 48,819 impressions, 1 click, average position 7.1, live #6.
   - Live top 10: six of seven rival titles use the plural, with lists of 10+ and 11 and first-hand proof ("I Compared", "I Use in Client Campaigns"). #1 already says 2027.
   - Ours: singular, opens on "Free", 7 tools.
   - Title: 7 Best Semrush Alternatives in 2026 (Free Tools Ranked) (55)

2. ahrefs alternatives, /blog/free-ahrefs-alternative: 40,009 impressions, 2 clicks, average position 8.9, live: not in the top 10.
   - The average position is wrong today, so this is a ranking problem before a title problem.
   - Live top 10: #1 lists 17 tools, and #4 owns our angle in the plural ("Free Ahrefs Alternatives in 2026: What Each Tool Replaces").
   - Title: 7 Free Ahrefs Alternatives Compared Side by Side (2026) (55)

3. moz alternatives, /blog/free-moz-pro-alternative: 39,246 impressions, 1 click, average position 2.7, live #3 (position confirmed).
   - Live top 10: every rival list says "Moz Alternatives", with 16 tools at #1 and "I Tested" below us.
   - Ours: "Moz Pro Alternative", singular, opens on "Free".
   - Title: 7 Best Moz Alternatives in 2026 (Free Tools Ranked) (51)

4. similarweb alternatives, /blog/free-similarweb-alternative: 6,679 impressions, 1 click, average position 5.5.
   - serp.md has no SERP for it, so the position is unverified and there is no rival comparison.
   - The same page gets 2 clicks on 3,434 impressions for "similarweb competitors", and its real clicks come from "free" queries, so the title keeps "Free".
   - Title: 7 Free Similarweb Alternatives and Competitors (2026) (53)

5. semrush alternative, same page as 1: 5,426 impressions, 16 clicks, average position 11.2 (page two on average).
   - No SERP in the file; the title from 1 covers it.

The single biggest reason (my inference from the numbers): most of these impressions are not people reading our snippet, because the same page, title and position earn 25% on "semrush best alternatives" (19 clicks on 76) and 0.0% on "semrush alternatives", so the title mismatch is only the fixable remainder.

And its closing line, word for word: "The four pages need plural, exact-match titles instead of "Free X Alternative", and Ahrefs must first get back into the top 10. Expect tens of extra clicks, not thousands: the head-term impressions look inflated."

Three things in this answer are why I pay for [top model] on this kind of job.

First, it found the real pattern. All four pages have the same title shape: "Free X Alternative", singular. People search "X alternatives", plural, and every rival title in the top 10 says it. That is one fix across four pages, not four separate problems.

Second, it refused to trust Search Console. Our average position on "ahrefs alternatives" says 8.9, so first page. The live results say we are not in the top 10 at all today. A cheaper model would have rewritten the title and called it done. [top model] said: this one is a ranking problem first, a new title will not save a page nobody sees. That is exactly the "never trust average position alone" rule from the CLAUDE.md, applied without me asking twice.

Third, it killed its own hype. "Expect tens of extra clicks, not thousands." It noticed that the same page, at the same position, with the same title, gets 25% clicks on "semrush best alternatives" and 0.0% on "semrush alternatives". So most of those 48,819 impressions are probably not humans reading our result. A junior would have promised you 40,000 new visitors. [top model] told me the truth, and the truth is what lets you decide where to spend your week.

What I am doing with it: the plural titles on the Semrush, Moz and Similarweb pages, and a separate job on the Ahrefs page to get it back into the top 10. I will post the numbers when there are numbers.

How to run it on your site tonight:

  • Export the last 28 days, queries and pages.
  • Search your top 3 non-brand queries in a private window and save each results page as text.
  • Put both in a folder, open Claude Code with [top model] at high effort, paste prompt 4.
  • Read the answer. Fix only what it says is fixable.

12. A keyword map in a file

The second most useful thing you can build: one file that says, for every query, which page should own it.

Most sites have no such map. So two blog posts fight for the same query, the product page ranks for an informational search it cannot win, and nobody knows which page to improve.

Prompt 5:

Read /data/gsc/queries-pages.tsv. Build keyword-map.csv with one row per query: query, intent (info, compare, buy, brand), impressions, clicks, the page that ranks today, the page that SHOULD rank (an existing URL or "new page").
Rules: one page per intent. When two of my pages show up for the same intent, flag it as cannibalisation with both URLs and their clicks.
Then write the 5 decisions I must make, the ones with the most clicks at stake first.

Two tips:

  • Let [light model] do the intent tagging first if you have thousands of queries (step 04), then give [top model] the tagged file. Same result, a fraction of the cost.
  • The "5 decisions" line matters more than the file. A map with 3,000 rows is a spreadsheet. Five decisions are a week of work you can actually do.

13. The whole audit with one word

Once a prompt works, stop pasting it. Claude Code lets you save a prompt as a command: a file in .claude/commands/ in your project. The file name becomes the command.

Save prompt 3 (the 4-model audit team of step 10) as .claude/commands/audit.md. From then on, you type:

/audit

and the whole team runs on whatever is in /data today.

Prompt 6 is the version I keep in that file, with one line added at the top so it compares with the last run:

Before anything: read /reports/last-audit.md if it exists, and list what changed since then (pages fixed, pages that got worse).
Then run the audit team as described below, and save the result to /reports/last-audit.md.
[paste prompt 3 here]

Now an audit is not a project anymore. It is a word you type every Monday.

14. Which pages lose clicks

When traffic drops, most people panic and change things. The first job is just to know where the clicks went, and whether it is a ranking problem or a snippet problem.

Export the pages report for two periods of 28 days (this one and the previous one), then prompt 7:

Compare period-a.csv and period-b.csv (Search Console, pages: clicks, impressions, ctr, position).
List the 10 pages that lost the most clicks. For each one:
- lost clicks and lost impressions
- impressions dropped too = a ranking problem; impressions stable and CTR dropped = a snippet or SERP problem
- the one check I should do first
Do not guess causes you cannot see in the data. Write "unknown" instead.

The impressions versus CTR split is the useful part:

  • Impressions down: Google shows you less. Look at rankings, at a competitor that moved, at an update.
  • Impressions stable, clicks down: Google shows you the same, people click less. Look at the results page: a new AI answer, new ads, a video block, a competitor's better title.

And the "unknown" line again. A model asked "why did traffic drop" with only Search Console data will invent a Google update. Make it say what it cannot see.

15. The overnight content refresh

This is the long job [top model] was built for, and the last promise of the intro.

Before bed, you hand it 5 pages that lose clicks (from step 14) or that sit on page two (from step 11). Prompt 8:

Refresh the 5 pages listed in refresh.txt. For each page:
1. Read the page, its Search Console queries (/data/gsc) and its live top 10 (/data/serp).
2. List what the top 3 results cover that my page does not.
3. Rewrite the page in /drafts/<slug>.md: keep what already ranks, add what is missing, new title and meta description.
4. Write changes.md: what changed on each page, and which query each change targets.
Finish the whole task. Do not stop to ask me questions: write your open questions at the end of changes.md.

"Finish the whole task" is not a style choice. Anthropic's own guide says to spell it out for long jobs like this one, so the model does not stop halfway to check in with you:

In the morning, you read changes.md, not 5 pages. You publish what you agree with, you throw away what you do not.

Two more prompts to finish the 10, because you will need them right after the refresh.

Prompt 9, the review before you publish (run it on [advanced model] or [top model], never on the model that wrote the draft):

Review /drafts/<slug>.md against the live top 10 in /data/serp/<slug>.md and the original page.
Flag: every claim without a source, every number I cannot verify, every section that answers a different question than the query.
Do not rewrite. Only list the problems, most serious first.

Prompt 10, the title test, for the pages of step 11:

For each page in titles.csv (page, current title, top 3 queries with impressions), write 3 title options under 60 characters.
Each option must contain the main query in the exact form people search it (singular or plural as in the data).
Pick the one you would ship and say why in one line.

That last rule is straight from this morning's run. Singular versus plural cost us thousands of impressions without a click.

A word on how to use prompts 9 and 10 together. Write with one model, review with another. When the same model writes a page and then reviews it, it tends to approve its own choices, because it reads its own reasoning as obvious. A second model has no such attachment. In my setup, [mid model] writes the draft, [top model] or [advanced model] reviews it with prompt 9, and only then do I read it. By the time a page reaches me, the made-up numbers and the off-topic sections are already flagged, and my job is the last judgment call: does this page say what we want our brand to say?

And keep the title test honest. Three options, one pick, one line of reason. If you ask for 20 titles, you will spend more time choosing than the change is worth.

5 mistakes that waste [top model] on SEO

I made most of these before writing this guide. They cost money, time, or both.

Mistake 1: no files, only questions.

"What should my SEO strategy be?" with nothing attached is the most expensive way to get a generic blog post. Every prompt in this guide starts with a file. If you have no file yet, your first job is the export, not the prompt.

Mistake 2: asking for ideas instead of decisions.

"Give me 30 content ideas" gets you 30 ideas and no way to choose. "Which 3 pages should I fix this week, and what is the expected effect" gets you a week of work. [top model] is good at deciding. Ask it to decide.

Mistake 3: trusting the numbers it did not read.

If a volume, a position or a click count appears in the answer and it was not in your files, it was invented. The CLAUDE.md of step 06 tells it to write "unknown" instead, and to name the file behind every number. Check one or two numbers anyway, every time. In the run of step 11, every figure matched our Search Console export.

Mistake 4: running everything on [top model].

The 4-model team of step 10 exists for a reason. [light model] tags, [mid model] extracts, [advanced model] checks, [top model] decides. If your bill is high and your output is the same as last month, look at which model did the volume work.

Mistake 5: shipping the output without reading it.

[top model] writes very good drafts and very confident recommendations. Both still go through you. In step 11, one of its five titles is for a page that is not even in the top 10 today, and it said so itself: changing that title alone would have done nothing. A human reading the answer catches that in ten seconds. A human skipping it ships a useless change and wonders why nothing moved.

the order I would do it in

You do not need all 15 steps on day one. Here is the order:

  • Evening 1: step 06 (the CLAUDE.md) and step 11 (quick wins). 30 minutes of setup, 2 minutes of [top model]. You get a list of pages to fix.
  • Week 1: fix the titles from step 11 with prompt 10. Do not touch anything else yet.
  • Week 2: step 12, the keyword map. Kill the cannibalisation it finds.
  • Week 3: step 15 on the 5 pages that matter most, with prompt 9 as the review.
  • Every Monday after that: step 13, /audit, and step 14 if the curve goes down.

And every time, [top model] at high effort for the thinking, cheaper models for the volume.

the questions I get every time

Do I need Claude Code, or does the chat work?

The chat works for steps 11, 12 and 14: upload the files, paste the prompt. Claude Code is better for anything with many files, subagents (steps 09 and 10) or saved commands (step 13).

Is [top model] worth it on a small site?

On a 10-page site with 200 impressions a month, honestly, [mid model] will do. [top model] shines when there is a lot of data to read and a real decision at the end.

Can it do the whole SEO without me?

No. It decides well on the data you give it. It does not know your margins, your sales team, or that a page exists for a partner. You stay the one who says yes.

What about rankings in ChatGPT and AI answers?

Same logic, different data: you hand it the answers you collected from the AI tools for your queries, and it tells you who gets cited and why. The prompts above work with that file in place of the SERP.

How long until I see a result?

A title change can show in Search Console within a few weeks, once Google recrawls the page and shows the new title. A content refresh usually takes longer. Measure the same query, on the same page, 28 days before and 28 days after, and nothing else.

Can I use it for a client site?

Yes, with their Search Console access and their go. Put the client's business, money pages and competitors in the CLAUDE.md, one folder per client, so their data never mixes with another client's.

Which file format does it read best?

Plain text and CSV or TSV. A screenshot of a table works, but it reads far fewer rows than an export, and you cannot check its numbers as easily. Always prefer the export.

what I did not test

  • I ran the quick-win prompt on one site (chatseo.app), one market (US results), one day.
  • I have not changed our titles yet. There is no "traffic went up" in this guide: the prompt found the problem, the result comes later. I will share it.
  • The live top 10 was read for our 3 biggest queries only, not all 5. The Google screenshots above come from a logged-in browser, so the order can differ from what you see.
  • I did not compare [top model] with another model on the same prompt and the same files.
  • The model split of step 04 is my setup, not a measured benchmark.
  • The "half the cost of [advanced model] at max" figure is Anthropic's own test, on code, not on SEO.

the point

[top model] is not a better chatbot. It is a senior SEO that needs your data and a clear job.

Give it files, not questions. Put it at high effort. Let cheaper models do the fetching. Make it decide on every page. And let it tell you what NOT to do: this morning, the most valuable sentence it wrote was "expect tens of extra clicks, not thousands".
